name: Mare Crisium
tip: Find the isolated oval sea near the eastern limb. Its foreshortened outline changes slightly with libration.

name: Mare Fecunditatis
tip: A broad, irregular sea south of Mare Crisium. Its western side contains the bright Messier crater pair; first trace the sea’s uneven border rather than expecting those tiny craters in binoculars.

name: Mare Frigoris
tip: Follow the long, narrow dark band across the northern Moon, above Plato and Mare Imbrium. Its stretched outline distinguishes it from the more rounded central seas.

name: Mare Humorum
tip: This compact, rounded basin lies in the southwest, with the crater Gassendi on its northern edge. Use that rim-side landmark to distinguish it from neighbouring Oceanus Procellarum.

name: Mare Imbrium
tip: Look for the broad northern sea. The darker patch of Plato and the curve of Sinus Iridum make useful landmarks.

name: Mare Nectaris
tip: Find the small, roughly oval sea south of Mare Tranquillitatis. The conspicuous Theophilus–Cyrillus–Catharina crater chain lies along its northwestern side.

name: Mare Nubium
tip: Look for the irregular southern sea west of Mare Nectaris. Bullialdus stands within its western part, while the Straight Wall is a much smaller telescopic feature near its eastern margin.

name: Oceanus Procellarum
tip: The Ocean of Storms spreads across the western near side without the neat circular outline of Mare Crisium. The bright Aristarchus region is a useful landmark along this vast dark expanse.

name: Mare Serenitatis
tip: A rounded sea immediately north of Mare Tranquillitatis. The two join through a narrower passage; compare their outlines and the contrast along Serenitatis’s darker rim.

name: Mare Tranquillitatis
tip: This irregular dark sea south of Serenitatis contains the Apollo 11 landing region near its southwest edge. The landing hardware is far too small for Earth-based binoculars.

name: Mare Vaporum
tip: A small central patch south of the Apennine Mountains, between the Imbrium and Serenitatis regions. Its modest size makes the neighbouring larger seas useful for identification.

name: Palus Epidemiarum
tip: Look for the dark plain against brighter highlands. Follow its outline rather than trying to resolve small surface details.

name: Palus Somni
tip: Look for the dark plain against brighter highlands. Follow its outline rather than trying to resolve small surface details.

name: Sinus Iridum
tip: Look for the curved bay opening onto Imbrium. Near the terminator, the rim can catch sunlight while the floor remains dark.

name: Sinus Medii
tip: Look for the dark plain against brighter highlands. Follow its outline rather than trying to resolve small surface details.

name: Sinus Roris
tip: Look for the dark plain against brighter highlands. Follow its outline rather than trying to resolve small surface details.

name: Atlas
tip: Find this crater beside Hercules in the northeastern highlands. Compare their paired outlines near the terminator; internal detail needs more magnification.

name: Cleomedes
tip: Look just north of Mare Crisium for this broad crater. Its rim is easiest near the terminator; the small craters on its floor need a telescope.

name: Endymion
tip: Seek a dark, foreshortened floor near the northeastern limb. Libration changes the view; steady binoculars help distinguish its outline.

name: Hercules
tip: Compare this crater with neighboring Atlas in the northeastern highlands. Look for the pair near the terminator rather than fine floor detail.

name: Langrenus
tip: Follow the eastern shore of Mare Fecunditatis to this prominent crater. Low sunlight makes the rim easier to pick out; use steady support.

name: Macrobius
tip: Search northwest of Mare Crisium for a broad crater rim in the highlands. The outline is a better binocular goal than its central peak.

name: Petavius
tip: Look southeast of Mare Fecunditatis, south of Langrenus. Seek its broad rim near the terminator; the famous floor rille is a telescope feature.

name: Vendelinus
tip: Find this worn crater between Langrenus and Petavius near the eastern limb. Look for its large outline in low sunlight, not a sharp bright ring.

name: Albategnius
tip: Search east of Ptolemaeus in the central highlands. Compare its rim with the surrounding cratered terrain near the terminator.

name: Aristillus
tip: Pair this crater with smaller Autolycus in eastern Mare Imbrium. Steady binoculars can show the bright pair; central peaks need a telescope.

name: Aristoteles
tip: Look for the northern member of the Aristoteles–Eudoxus pair beside Mare Frigoris. Compare the two rims in low sunlight.

name: Autolycus
tip: Seek the smaller crater south of Aristillus in eastern Mare Imbrium. Start with the pair as bright patches before trying their separate outlines.

name: Cassini
tip: Find this small flooded crater in northern Mare Imbrium, near the lunar Alps. Its outline is a mounted-binocular challenge; interior craters need a telescope.

name: Catharina
tip: Follow the Theophilus–Cyrillus–Catharina chain southward beside Mare Nectaris. This is the southern, more worn member; compare the broad outlines.

name: Cyrillus
tip: Identify the middle member of the Theophilus–Cyrillus–Catharina chain beside Mare Nectaris. The overlapping rims are best near the terminator.

name: Eudoxus
tip: Look south of Aristoteles for the smaller member of this northern crater pair. A braced view helps separate the two outlines.

name: Fracastorius
tip: Inspect the southern edge of Mare Nectaris for a partly flooded crater. Its open northern rim blends into the mare; low sunlight helps trace the southern arc.

name: Hipparchus
tip: Search northeast of Ptolemaeus for a large, worn crater plain. Seek the broad irregular boundary near the terminator rather than a crisp ring.

name: Maurolycus
tip: Look in the crowded southeastern highlands for this broad crater. Low sunlight and mounted binoculars help distinguish it from neighboring rims.

name: Piccolomini
tip: Search southeast of Mare Nectaris for a distinct crater near the southern end of Rupes Altai. The rim is the binocular goal; its central peak needs more power.

name: Posidonius
tip: Trace the northeastern shore of Mare Serenitatis to this broad flooded crater. Look for its oval outline; the intricate floor is a telescope subject.

name: Theophilus
tip: Identify the northern member of the Theophilus–Cyrillus–Catharina chain beside Nectaris. Look for the outline rather than fine interior detail.

name: Alphonsus
tip: Follow the central chain south from Ptolemaeus to Alphonsus and then Arzachel. Compare their sizes and outlines near the terminator.

name: Archimedes
tip: Find the broad, dark-floored crater in southern Mare Imbrium. Compare its smooth-looking floor with the smaller Aristillus–Autolycus pair to the east.

name: Arzachel
tip: Identify the southern member of the Ptolemaeus–Alphonsus–Arzachel chain. Its compact rim is easier to distinguish with steady support and low sunlight.

name: Bullialdus
tip: Search western Mare Nubium for this conspicuous crater. Look for a bright rim and shadow near the terminator; central peaks need a telescope.

name: Clavius
tip: A large indentation in the southern highlands is the binocular goal near the terminator. The internal crater chain is a telescope challenge.

name: Copernicus
tip: Identify the bright patch in the western half. Near full Moon, trace its ray halo; at low power, do not expect the central peaks to resolve.

name: Eratosthenes
tip: Follow the Apennine mountains to their southwestern end. This crater marks the end of the arc; low sunlight makes the rim easier to recognize.

name: Gassendi
tip: Find the large crater on the northern shore of Mare Humorum. Compare its oval boundary with the dark mare; floor fractures need a telescope.

name: Longomontanus
tip: Search west of Tycho in the southern highlands for this large, worn crater. Its broad outline is best near the terminator.

name: Maginus
tip: Look east of Clavius for this large, battered crater in the southern highlands. Low sunlight helps separate its worn rim from surrounding craters.

name: Plato
tip: Seek the dark oval at the northern edge of Imbrium. Its floor is recognizable; the tiny craterlets require much more magnification.

name: Ptolemaeus
tip: Follow the large crater outline in the central southern highlands near the terminator; compare it with Alphonsus and Arzachel below.

name: Tycho
tip: Follow the long pale rays across the southern highlands near full Moon. The ray system is much easier than details inside this small crater.

name: Walther
tip: Search the south-central highlands for this broad crater among overlapping rims. A mounted view near the terminator is more useful than full-Moon lighting.

name: Aristarchus
tip: Find an unusually bright patch in the western maria. The crater and nearby plateau blend together at low magnification.

name: Grimaldi
tip: Look for the dark, foreshortened oval near the western limb. A steady support helps separate it from surrounding highlands.

name: Kepler
tip: Find the small bright patch west of Copernicus. Its ray halo is easier to recognize than the crater itself in ordinary binoculars.
